items.stem: A pharmacy completes a paper DEA Form 222 with 21 separate Schedule II line items on the same form. All quantities and supplier details are otherwise accurate. What must change?

choices.text: Keep 21 lines if a second pharmacist signs.
choices.why: Additional signers do not override the form's line-item maximum.

choices.text: Combine unrelated finished dosage forms into a single item.
choices.why: An order line must describe the same finished or bulk form and quantity; distinct products cannot be hidden under one line.

choices.text: Use an additional DEA Form 222 for the extra item.
choices.why: The current form permits no more than 20 line items; a new form is needed for item 21.

choices.text: Use the back of Form 222 for unlimited additional items.
choices.why: DEA's prescribed form limits line items instead of permitting an unlimited reverse-side continuation.

items.stem: The supplier receives a paper Form 222 with an erased drug strength and a handwritten correction. The actual intended order is clear from a telephone call. Which action is authorized?

choices.text: Ship the product after marking the correction with the supplier's initials.
choices.why: A defective paper order cannot be repaired by the supplier.

choices.text: Return the defective order with a reason; the purchaser must execute a new Form 222.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1305.15 expressly bars filling altered orders and bars correction of the defective form.

choices.text: Have the purchaser telephone the quantity to create an emergency Form 222.
choices.why: An informal call is not the required replacement controlled-substance order.

choices.text: Supply a smaller quantity from the altered order.
choices.why: A defective Form 222 cannot be partially filled merely because a smaller amount is requested.

items.stem: Supplier S cannot fill a Schedule II order and properly endorses its untouched DEA Form 222 to Supplier T. Which distribution scenario is allowed under the endorsement rule?

choices.text: Only T fills the endorsed order and ships it directly to the original purchaser.
choices.why: After endorsement, the first supplier may not fill any part; the second supplier may fill and ship directly to purchaser.

choices.text: S fills half while T fills the rest.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1305.14 prohibits the first supplier from fulfilling any part after endorsement.

choices.text: T ships the containers to S for repackaging before delivery.
choices.why: The endorsed-order provisions require shipment directly to the original purchaser.

choices.text: The purchaser endorses the form after S declines.
choices.why: Only the supplier to whom the original Form 222 was made out may endorse it.

items.stem: A registered distributor's CSOS software detects that the DEA digital certificate used to SIGN a Schedule II electronic order had already expired before signature. Which response follows the federal rule?

choices.text: Accept because the receiving pharmacy is a current DEA registrant.
choices.why: Current pharmacy registration does not validate an order signed with an expired certificate.

choices.text: Have the supplier edit the certificate timestamp and reprocess.
choices.why: Neither party may correct a defective electronic order.

choices.text: Print the invalid electronic order and treat it as a signed paper Form 222.
choices.why: A printout does not cure a failed digitally signed order.

choices.text: Reject the invalid order, notify the purchaser, and require a newly executed valid order.
choices.why: Expired-before-signature certificates disqualify the order under 21 CFR 1305.25.

items.stem: DEA issues a final rule controlling an existing, formerly nonscheduled medicine effective December 1. A pharmacy already stocks it. Which federal controlled inventory step is due on the effective date?

choices.text: Record it for the first time only at the pharmacy's next ordinary biennial inventory.
choices.why: Newly scheduled substances have a special inventory timing rule in addition to ordinary biennial inventories.

choices.text: Inventory the on-hand substance as of its effective scheduling date.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1304.11(d) requires an inventory on the effective date when a previously uncontrolled substance becomes scheduled.

choices.text: Dispose of all on-hand product instead of inventorying it.
choices.why: DEA scheduling does not by itself mandate discarding otherwise lawful stock.

choices.text: Count only packages received after the new scheduling order becomes effective.
choices.why: The on-hand inventory includes preexisting stock newly subject to control.

items.stem: A DEA-registered pharmacy keeps Schedule II acquisition records intermixed with Schedule III–V files and says any electronically searchable index eliminates all separation requirements. Which federal record system is required?

choices.text: One unsorted folder for every controlled schedule is sufficient if the pharmacy's finance manager can eventually locate an invoice.
choices.why: Schedule II records must be kept separate rather than merely retrievable with effort.

choices.text: All Schedule III–V records must be filed separately from one another, with their own DEA facility registration.
choices.why: For Schedule III–V, separate storage or readily retrievable records suffice; individual separate registrations are not required.

choices.text: Separate Schedule II records from other records; keep Schedule III–V records separate or readily retrievable.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1304.04(h) distinguishes strict Schedule II separation from the Schedule III–V alternative.

choices.text: Dispose of invoices after the computerized purchasing balance is reconciled.
choices.why: DEA acquisition and inventory records must be retained under federal and applicable state rules.

items.stem: At the federal biennial inventory, the pharmacy has a partially filled Schedule IV bottle originally containing 1,500 tablets and a partially filled Schedule II bottle originally containing 100 tablets. Which counting rule applies?

choices.text: Estimate the remaining count in both.
choices.why: Schedule II quantities require an exact count.

choices.text: Estimate Schedule IV because it is not Schedule II, and count Schedule II exactly.
choices.why: A Schedule III–V container holding more than 1,000 tablets or capsules requires an exact count.

choices.text: Count both exactly.
choices.why: Schedule II always requires an exact count; the >1,000 tablet Schedule IV container also does.

choices.text: Count only unopened bottles.
choices.why: The inventory must include all controlled substances on hand, including opened containers.

items.stem: A newly registered retail pharmacy opens for business on Monday with zero federally controlled substances physically present or under its control. Its first Schedule III shipment will arrive Friday. What initial DEA inventory entry is required?

choices.text: Document an initial inventory of zero on Monday; subsequently record controlled-drug receipts.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1304.11(b) requires an initial inventory on first engaging in registered activity, including an affirmative zero record.

choices.text: Delay the initial inventory until Friday when stock arrives.
choices.why: A zero-stock first-business-day inventory is still required.

choices.text: Mark all future stock as on hand on Monday.
choices.why: An inventory must reflect actual controlled substances on hand at the specified time.

choices.text: Wait two years for the first inventory because no controlled product was stocked at opening.
choices.why: The biennial inventory follows, rather than replaces, the initial inventory.

items.stem: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy CONFIRMS an employee stole one tablet of a Schedule IV medication this afternoon. The pharmacist asks whether the small quantity eliminates Board reporting. Which action is required?

choices.text: Omit reporting because one tablet cannot be significant.
choices.why: Board Policy 2026-01 covers ALL confirmed employee pilferage regardless of amount.

choices.text: Report to the Board only if the medication is Schedule II.
choices.why: The confirmed theft category includes every controlled schedule.

choices.text: Wait for a criminal conviction before filing.
choices.why: The policy addresses confirmed theft/diversion rather than a final criminal conviction.

choices.text: File the Board RLCS report within seven calendar days and comply with applicable DEA and police duties.
choices.why: The Board's deadline and report apply to any confirmed theft; federal obligations are independent.

items.stem: A pharmacy detects a two-tablet Schedule II perpetual-inventory discrepancy. A documented receiving error is plausible, so it has not determined whether a true loss or theft occurred. What is the safest legally supported next step?

choices.text: Automatically report two tablets as confirmed employee diversion without investigating.
choices.why: The initial discrepancy is not proof of a particular cause or a confirmed theft.

choices.text: Secure the stock and investigate/reconcile promptly; determine reporting duties using actual findings.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.21 requires MOR investigation, while federal significant-loss and Board confirmed-loss thresholds must be assessed.

choices.text: Erase the discrepancy and restart the inventory without documentation.
choices.why: Editing away unexplained quantities defeats the reconciliation requirement.

choices.text: Ignore the issue unless the next biennial count also differs.
choices.why: MA requires ongoing reconciliation and investigation rather than biennial deferral.

items.stem: A licensed Massachusetts hospital pharmacy's nursing unit notices a likely missing Schedule II dose; hospital investigation is underway and theft is suspected but not yet proven. What reporting rule applies to this health-care facility?

choices.text: Apply only the community-pharmacy Board RLCS procedure and defer all other communication.
choices.why: The facility-specific DCP guidelines impose distinct reporting duties.

choices.text: Submit DEA Form 106 and ignore Massachusetts reporting until the investigation is finished.
choices.why: Federal forms do not displace the health-care facility's immediate state notification.

choices.text: Notify Massachusetts DPH Drug Control Program immediately upon discovery and follow its facility reporting process.
choices.why: The state's hospital/clinic accountability guidance requires immediate DCP reporting of suspected or confirmed theft/loss.

choices.text: Wait for the next weekly nursing-unit audit before informing anyone.
choices.why: Weekly QA reviews do not defer immediate suspected-theft/loss reporting.

items.stem: A DEA-registered Massachusetts retail pharmacy confirms a reportable Schedule II theft on Monday, November 2, 2026. There are no holidays. Which timing statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The federal initial written DEA field-division notice is due within one business day of discovery.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1301.76(b) specifies one business day for initial federal notice.

choices.text: The Massachusetts Board RLCS report must be submitted within one business day.
choices.why: The Board Policy 2026-01 deadline is seven calendar days, not the DEA initial-notice clock.

choices.text: The DEA Form 106 must be filed within 45 days of discovery through the federal secure network.
choices.why: This separate 45-day federal Form 106 deadline appears in 21 CFR 1301.76(b).

choices.text: The resident pharmacy must submit the Board RLCS and Form 106 if applicable within seven calendar days of the confirmed event.
choices.why: Board Policy 2026-01 has its own seven-calendar-day reporting process.

items.stem: At a DEA-authorized collection receptacle in a registered Massachusetts pharmacy, an ultimate user arrives with their lawfully held Schedule II tablets. They offer the closed bottle to a pharmacy technician to count before putting it in the receptacle. What is required?

choices.text: Technician counts every tablet, writes a return prescription entry, then deposits them.
choices.why: Collector staff may not individually handle, count, or inventory the ultimate-user drugs after collection; the user deposits them.

choices.text: Have the ultimate user deposit the medication directly into the authorized receptacle without employee handoff or counting.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1317.75(c) forbids transferring collected substances to another person and prohibits postdeposit individual handling.

choices.text: Place the product in the pharmacy's own expired Schedule II inventory.
choices.why: Ultimate-user property entering an authorized collection is not pharmacy-owned saleable stock.

choices.text: Return controlled drugs to the patient because collectors may accept only noncontrolled drugs.
choices.why: Authorized collectors may take lawfully held ultimate-user Schedule II–V medications.

items.stem: At a DEA-authorized pharmacy collection receptacle, a filled removable inner liner is removed by two collector employees. One wants to unseal and sort the tablets before shipping the liner for destruction. Which procedure complies?

choices.text: Seal it immediately under the two-employee process, retain identification and never reopen or sort its contents.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1317.60(c) requires immediate two-employee sealing and forbids reopening, x-raying or analyzing the sealed liner.

choices.text: Sort pills to determine whether a Schedule II Form 222 is needed for the returned patient tablets.
choices.why: After collection the liner's contents may not be sorted and patient take-back does not create an ordinary purchase order.

choices.text: Store the unsealed inner liner in an office desk until the next business day.
choices.why: The regulation requires sealing immediately upon removal.

choices.text: Combine the liner with the pharmacy's defective inventory and treat it as an ordinary purchase return.
choices.why: A collected ultimate-user liner is not the registrant's pharmacy inventory.

items.stem: A registered pharmacy lawfully destroys its own expired Schedule III stock on-site using an approved method and two authorized employee witnesses. Which statements describe the federal destruction record? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Form 41 is never needed because the substance is Schedule III rather than II.
choices.why: Registrant destruction recordkeeping extends beyond Schedule II.

choices.text: The two authorized witnesses document that they observed the destruction.

choices.text: Send the Form 41 to DEA automatically after every destruction, without exception.
choices.why: The current DEA Form 41 instructions say retention is generally required, submission only on request.

choices.text: Retain the destruction record for at least two years and make it available to DEA upon request.
choices.why: The DEA Form 41 instructions apply the federal at-least-two-year record retention requirement.

items.stem: A registered pharmacy moves its DEA-authorized collection receptacle next to an unattended front entrance so customers may deposit Schedule II medicine after the pharmacy closes. Which action is supported by 21 CFR 1317.75?

choices.text: Allow the receptacle to remain open after hours if it is permanently bolted down.

choices.text: Allow the store security guard to open the liner at closing to inventory deposited pills.

choices.why: The regulation requires supervised location and limits access during periods without employee monitoring.

choices.text: Accept all Schedule I–VI controlled substances since the receptacle has an inner liner.

choices.text: The state pays every inspection expense, even when investigating a licensed nonresident applicant.

choices.text: The nearest Massachusetts retail competitor pays the costs because it serves the same patients.

choices.text: Only DEA may inspect an out-of-state facility, so the Board cannot inspect any records.
choices.why: Massachusetts oversight of its nonresident licensee is not displaced by federal DEA authority.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy keeps electronic Schedule III–V prescription records on a contracted cloud server. DEA requests inspection and a readable export at the registered pharmacy. What response is required?

choices.text: Refuse because electronically stored prescriptions may be inspected only at the cloud provider's headquarters.
choices.why: 21 CFR 1304.04(h)(5) requires ready retrieval at the pharmacy's registered location.

choices.text: Print a monthly aggregate total with no patient, drug, prescriber or fill information.

choices.text: Produce sortable, readable prescription records at the registered location, even if server hardware is elsewhere.
choices.why: The e-prescription application must support prompt inspection, printing or transfer and sorting by required fields.

choices.text: Destroy electronic records after 30 days when the patient receives the medication.
choices.why: Federal records have an at-least-two-year period and applicable state rules may be longer.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy's security video showing routine stock activity is 20 days old. Separate footage covers a suspected controlled-substance theft from 11 months ago. Which retention rule is correctly stated?

choices.text: Every video must be destroyed after exactly 14 days.
choices.why: Fourteen days is a general minimum, not a mandatory deletion date; theft footage has a longer rule.

choices.text: Keep all surveillance video forever.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.21 specifies minimum periods rather than perpetual retention.

choices.text: Delete suspected-theft footage after 14 days if no police report was made.
choices.why: Known or suspected theft/diversion triggers a two-year minimum retention.

choices.text: Keep known or suspected theft/diversion footage at least two years; ordinary footage at least fourteen days.
choices.why: 247 CMR 9.21(4) differentiates routine and known/suspected diversion video records.
